### Inventory established before synthesis

Title: **Defeating Prompt Injections by Design**. Authors: Edoardo Debenedetti, Ilia Shumailov, Tianqi Fan, Jamie Hayes, Nicholas Carlini, Daniel Fabian, Christoph Kern, Chongyang Shi, Andreas Terzis, and Florian Tramèr. Affiliations: Google, Google DeepMind, and ETH Zurich. The supplied version is arXiv:2503.18813v2, dated 24 June 2025, category cs.CR. A separate publication venue is not specified on the supplied title page. Document type: a mixed cybersecurity and computer-systems paper with AI-agent experiments, a formal security-game definition, implementation details, and qualitative attack analyses. It is not a systematic review and does not report a controlled standalone-LLM versus web-agent comparison.

The inventory comprises the abstract; main sections S1–S11; design subsections SS5.1–SS5.4; evaluation subsections SS6.1–SS6.5, including SS6.1.1–SS6.1.3 and SS6.2.1–SS6.2.2; discussion subsections SS9.1–SS9.3; appendices A–I and their named subsections; Figures F1–F21; Tables T1–T14; security-game algorithm ALG1 in F3; policy-checked execution algorithm ALG2 in F4; dependency and side-channel mathematical concepts; eight illustrative failure categories; eight detailed failure examples H.4.1–H.4.8; and the expanded side-channel in Appendix I. No numbered theorem, lemma, formal hypothesis, or explicitly numbered research question is present. Seven footnotes explain the acronym, capability meaning, approval boundary, formal allowed-action set, privacy analogy, malware analogy, and control/data distinction.

## 1. Plain-language orientation

[A] This paper studies an AI assistant that can do things: retrieve documents, read messages, send emails, update calendars, and make payments through tools. Such an assistant encounters information that its user did not write and cannot fully trust. An attacker can place malicious instructions in that information. If the assistant treats those instructions as authoritative, a legitimate task can turn into data theft or another unauthorized action.

The proposed defense, **CaMeL**, means **CApabilities for MachinE Learning**. Instead of depending on a language model to recognize every attack, CaMeL surrounds the model with a software layer that separates planning from reading untrusted content, tracks where values came from, and checks rules before tools act. A model can still misunderstand malicious text; the surrounding system attempts to prevent that misunderstanding from crossing a protected security boundary.

[A] The central example is sending Bob a document named in meeting notes. Protecting the overall sequence—read notes, extract details, retrieve a document, send email—is insufficient. An attacker can preserve that sequence while changing the extracted document name and recipient. CaMeL therefore protects both **control flow**, the sequence and selection of actions, and **data flow**, the information supplied to those actions (pp. 2–4).

[A] The abstract reports approximately 77% task completion with security guarantees versus approximately 84% for an undefended system. Table 2 gives the corresponding o3 High values as 77.3% ± 8.3 and 84.5% ± 7.2. Other model results are less favorable for utility, and benchmark attack counts are not universally zero. The authors explicitly acknowledge side channels, policy-maintenance burdens, excluded text-only attacks, and the absence of a formally verified implementation. These conditions are essential to interpreting the contribution.

[D, MEDIUM] For the user's research question, the paper explains why tool-using web agents can expose more dangerous pathways than a text-only model: outside content can influence operations involving privileged data and external services. It does not quantify an intrinsic difference in model susceptibility between agents and standalone LLMs. Its strongest relevance is architectural and causal, not a measured relative-vulnerability estimate.

## 2. Document roadmap

Sections 1–2 introduce the problem, motivating example, and insufficiency of isolation alone. Section 3 defines the main attacker and explicit non-goals. Section 4 formalizes success and failure through the PI-SEC security game. Section 5 explains the architecture: two model roles, security policies, capabilities, and the interpreter. Section 6 measures utility, security, policy-triggering frequency, baseline performance, and token overhead; it also examines how apparently fixed plans can become general instruction interpreters. Section 7 analyzes three side-channel mechanisms. Section 8 extends the discussion to spy tools and rogue users. Section 9 considers adoption, declassification, user fatigue, and why neither prompt injection nor AgentDojo is fully solved. Sections 10–11 propose future work and conclude.

Appendix A supplies terminology and related-work positioning. B contains model utility and attack tables. C contains baseline comparisons. D contrasts NORMAL and STRICT modes. E lists evaluated policies. F gives token overhead and token-count tables. G maps failure categories to individual tasks. H reproduces the planning prompt, repair prompt, generated dispatch examples, and eight failure transcripts. I expands the exception-based side-channel into a realistic meeting-summary task. The acknowledgments and author-contribution statement on pp. 25–26 are administrative material; the references on pp. 27–30 establish the authors' cited context but were not independently validated.

## 3. Background and context

[A] A **large language model**, or LLM, produces and interprets text. In a **tool-calling agent**, model-produced requests are interpreted by a runtime as calls to an **application programming interface**, or API. The runtime executes the operation and returns its output to the model, which may choose another call. Appendix A.1.3 describes this feedback loop. The returned information becomes an attack surface because it can contain instructions written by someone other than the user.

A **prompt injection** inserts attacker-controlled instructions into content the model processes. The paper emphasizes untrusted emails, documents, spreadsheets, web pages, and tool outputs. **Exfiltration** means sending private information to a recipient who is not authorized to receive it. **Integrity** concerns preserving intended execution or state; **confidentiality** concerns keeping protected information from unauthorized observers.

[A] **Control Flow Integrity**, or CFI, restricts execution to permitted paths. **Information Flow Control**, or IFC, tracks information and restricts its movement into unauthorized contexts. **Access control** governs access to resources. CaMeL combines these ideas at the agent-system boundary rather than attempting to describe all internal neural-model computations.

[A] A **capability** is a security tag or token describing fine-grained rights. In CaMeL's current implementation, each value carries provenance and permitted-reader information. This use of capability is unrelated to a model's general skill level. **Provenance** records origin: user literals, interpreter transformations, tool outputs, and sometimes inner sources such as email senders. **Readers** are either Public or a set of users identified, for example, by email addresses (p. 9).

[A] **Structured output** makes a model return fields conforming to a specified schema. It constrains shape, not truth or authorization. The paper's quarantined model can return an attacker-chosen but structurally valid email address. That distinction explains why schemas and isolation need additional policy enforcement. **Side channels** reveal information through observable behavior—request counts, termination, or timing—rather than directly placing a secret in a tool argument.

## 4. Research problem and gap

**Existing problem [A].** Agents must process untrusted information to fulfill useful tasks, while their tools can access private resources or change the world. Malicious instructions embedded in that information can redirect actions or information flows (pp. 1–4).

**Shortcomings attributed to previous approaches [A].** Prompt reminders, delimiters, fine-tuning, instruction hierarchy, and related heuristic defenses ask the model itself to distinguish authorized instructions from malicious content. The authors state that these approaches do not provide security guarantees. Their discussion of outside work is author-reported positioning, not independent verification of the cited literature.

**Research gap [A].** The Dual LLM pattern protects planning by preventing a privileged planner from reading untrusted content. It does not by itself prevent an untrusted parser's output from becoming dangerous tool arguments. Nor does a fixed generated plan guarantee that attacker-controlled values cannot choose among many prewritten action branches. The missing protection is explicit, enforceable control over the use and propagation of individual values.

**Motivation and scope [A].** The authors seek a practical system that can enforce security policies even if underlying models remain vulnerable. They evaluate this on AgentDojo, covering Workspace, Banking, Travel, and Slack. The scope is agentic tool calling, not all harmful outputs from all models. No open-web crawler experiment or standalone-model comparison is reported.

[D, MEDIUM] The research question is best decomposed into increased exposure and increased consequence. An agent encounters more external content during its workflow, and its tools can turn a misleading interpretation into an operation on protected assets. The paper directly supports those mechanisms; a universal claim that every web agent is more vulnerable than every standalone LLM would exceed its evidence.

## 5. Research questions / objectives / hypotheses

The paper does not state formal research questions or statistical hypotheses. Its explicit objectives and contributions are to design CaMeL without changing the underlying model, extract control/data flows from user queries, implement a provenance-tracking interpreter, enforce explicit policies, and integrate the system with AgentDojo (p. 2).

The following are **analyst-organized evaluation questions**, not quoted author RQs:

- O1: Can separating trusted planning from untrusted parsing reduce successful agent attacks?
- O2: Can fine-grained capabilities and tool-time policies close gaps left by isolation?
- O3: How much useful task completion remains under benign and adversarial conditions?
- O4: Which task structures and implementation issues cause failures?
- O5: Can a cheaper quarantined model reduce cost without much utility loss?
- O6: What additional security and usability costs accompany STRICT dependency tracking?
- O7: Which side channels and deployment burdens remain?

The user's standalone-versus-web-agent question is a research-use lens applied to the paper. It is not one of the paper's experimentally tested hypotheses. Confidence in that distinction is HIGH.

## 6. Assumptions / threat model

[A] In the main threat model, the user's prompt is trusted. The user is not pasting an attacker-written prompt, and any agent memory is assumed uncompromised (p. 5). An adversary can introduce or modify data that the agent retrieves, such as an email, shared document, or spreadsheet. The adversary seeks an action outside the allowed set for the user prompt, including a wrong payment, unauthorized disclosure, or other prohibited operation.

The privileged planner receives the trusted query and tool descriptions, but not tool-result contents or quarantined-model outputs. The quarantined parser reads potentially malicious content but has no tool access. The interpreter, capability propagation, source annotations, and security policies form the enforcement boundary. [D] The resulting argument depends on those components behaving correctly; the paper itself proposes formal verification as future work rather than demonstrating that the implementation is fault-free.

[A] Excluded attacks include text-to-text manipulation without protected-flow consequences, such as a false summary, and phishing through displayed content. CaMeL can attach origin information to displayed text, but preventing those persuasive or semantic errors is not its main goal. Full autonomy is also not promised: ambiguous requests or policy-denied actions can require human clarification or approval.

[A] Sections 8–9 discuss stronger adversaries: malicious tools, compromised users, and insiders violating organizational policy. Those scenarios are conceptual extensions, not AgentDojo evaluations. A deployment using organizational policies must not assume that user-originated literals automatically override every corporate restriction. The paper's trusted-user main model and stronger-user scenario need separate interpretation.

[A] Side-channel leakage is explicitly acknowledged. STRICT mode mitigates particular implicit-flow and Q-LLM exception channels, but arbitrary tool-induced exceptions and other timing channels may remain. Consequently, the claim is conditional policy enforcement and improved isolation, not universal secrecy against every observation.

## 7. Methodology

### Architecture and workflow

[A] CaMeL uses six components: Privileged LLM (P-LLM), Quarantined LLM (Q-LLM), tools, security policies, per-value capabilities, and a custom interpreter (pp. 6–10). The P-LLM converts a natural-language task into restricted Python-like code. It can reference tools and invoke the Q-LLM as a function, specifying a Pydantic schema for each extraction. Returned contents reside in runtime variables, invisible to the P-LLM.

The Q-LLM returns structured data and an added boolean, `have_enough_information`. False causes a `NotEnoughInformationError`. It cannot tell the P-LLM which information is missing because that message could transport an injection. This deliberate restriction protects the boundary while creating a recovery bottleneck. The P-LLM can revise code from error location/type and trusted context, but cannot inspect the secret or untrusted variable contents directly.

The interpreter parses code with Python's abstract syntax tree library, recursively interprets supported nodes, tracks dependencies, propagates provenance/readers, and checks policies before tools execute. If `c = a + b`, c depends on both a and b. Policies inspect tool arguments and their dependency ancestors. Python was chosen because it is familiar and models write it competently; policies use Python rather than a custom domain-specific language to allow flexible logic.

### Policies and capabilities

[A] Each policy takes a tool name and arguments and returns Allowed or Denied with a reason. A calendar-event policy can permit sharing when participants originate from the trusted user; otherwise, it checks that participants can read the title and other event fields. This is an actual policy exception, not an unconditional statement that every event field must already be shared. Data annotations and access granularity are use-case dependent.

Sources include User for generated-code literals, CaMeL for transformations, unique tools, and optional inner sources. Readers are Public or explicit user sets. The passport-versus-telephone example on p. 9 illustrates why coarse rules such as allowing all personally identifiable information into a restaurant tool are inadequate. The paper does not provide a full algebra of every capability operation or a proof of propagation correctness.

### Interpreter restrictions and recovery

[A] Appendix H.1 disallows imports, `eval`, `exec`, while loops, generators, break/continue, new functions, and mutable methods such as list append. It provides selected built-ins, string/dictionary methods, date/time classes, schema classes, and tool signatures. The supplied transcripts additionally reveal unsupported slices and try blocks. `type` returns a type-name string rather than a Python type object. These details make this a custom language dialect, not unrestricted Python execution.

[A] The system prompts the P-LLM up to 10 times to obtain runnable code. Error text depending on untrusted data is redacted. Variables, classes, dependencies, and capabilities persist across attempts. Already executed side effects should not be repeated. There is no transaction atomicity or rollback for partially executed instruction sequences (p. 10). Appendix H.2 shows both the repair prompt and the redaction message.

### NORMAL and STRICT modes

[A] NORMAL tracks explicit data dependencies. STRICT also propagates dependence on conditional tests and loop iterables, addressing implicit flows. After a Q-LLM call, STRICT makes subsequent statements depend on that call's inputs to reduce exception-based leakage. This increases the number of policy triggers. Neither mode is demonstrated as a universal side-channel solution.

### Evaluation configuration and reporting limits

[A] AgentDojo supplies tasks in four suites. Table 1's failure analysis includes 40 Workspace, 16 Banking, 20 Slack, and 20 Travel tasks. [C] Their sum is 96, and 62 correct corresponds to 62/96 = 64.58%; this must not silently replace Table 5's 63.92%, which belongs to a differently represented evaluation. Security figures report 949 attacks. The supplied work does not fully describe attack-family construction, run repetitions, random seeds, confidence-interval computation, hardware, API parameters, or benchmark revision.

[A] Section 6.1 lists Gemini 2.5 Flash preview 05-20, Gemini 2.5 Pro preview 05-06, Claude 3.5 Haiku 20241022, Claude Sonnet 4 with/without a 16,000 reasoning-token budget, GPT-4.1 2025-04-14, o4-mini 2025-04-16 High, and o3 2025-04-16 High. The printed Claude Sonnet 4 identifier includes `20241022`; this is reproduced as supplied and not externally corrected. Tables 2–4 show six principal model conditions, not every model mentioned in the prose.

Utility is benchmark task success; security is attacker-goal success. Policies are evaluated separately through triggering rates. Token estimates use GPT-4o's tokenizer via tiktoken because Claude's tokenizer is unavailable, exclude tool-documentation tokens, and include the CaMeL language-specification prompt. No train/validation/test split or new model training is reported.

## 8. Experiments / analyses

### X1 — Benign utility across models

[A] Native provider tool calling is compared with CaMeL across the four suites (Fig. 8, Table 2, pp. 12, 33). Overall native/CaMeL utility is 86.6/74.2 for Claude 4 Sonnet; 83.5/70.1 with reasoning; 55.7/35.1 for Gemini Flash; 73.2/41.2 for Gemini Pro; 84.5/77.3 for o3 High; and 79.4/76.3 for o4 Mini High, all percentages. Table uncertainty terms are retained in sections 9 and 20. The manipulated condition is execution architecture, not standalone-versus-agent status: both alternatives are agents.

CaMeL sometimes improves a suite result: o3 Banking is 81.2% versus 62.5%, and o4 Travel is 75.0% versus 65.0%. Conversely, Gemini models reach 0.0% CaMeL Travel utility, and Slack drops substantially for all six. These heterogeneous results qualify the authors' characterization of a small utility impact.

### X2 — Failure-mode analysis

[A/B] Claude 3.5 Sonnet failures are categorized in Tables 1 and 14, supported by Appendix H.4 transcripts. Counts are one query misunderstanding, five data-requires-action, three wrong assumptions, five insufficient-context, three overdoing/strict-evaluation, one ambiguous task, thirteen underdocumented-API, and three benchmark-bug instances. Correct counts are 31/40 Workspace, 12/16 Banking, 14/20 Slack, and 5/20 Travel. The caption says two misunderstandings while the row shows one; this discrepancy remains unresolved.

### X3 — Lower-cost Q-LLM substitution

[A] Claude 3.5 Haiku as Q-LLM with Claude 4 Sonnet as P-LLM reportedly reduces utility by about 1% and estimated median-task cost by 12%. GPT-4.1 Nano with o4 Mini High reportedly has a similar utility drop (p. 12). Exact tables, sample counts, prices, and uncertainty for this substitution are not supplied. The paper does not clarify whether approximately 1% means relative percent or percentage points.

### X4 — Attacks without added policies

[A] CaMeL isolation alone is compared with native calling under 949 benchmark attacks (Fig. 9, Tables 3–4). Table 4 reports Gemini Pro native 163 ± 140.1 successful attacks versus 0 ± 0.0 under either CaMeL condition. Main text instead says 300 to 0; the figure visually resembles that larger value. These must remain distinct reports. Residual no-policy successes include banking instructions in a user-requested document and displayed hotel-review content; the authors classify these as outside their principal threat model.

### X5 — Added policy enforcement

[A] Policies are added to the isolated architecture, and policy-trigger rates are examined for Gemini Pro, reasoning Claude Sonnet 4, and o3 High (Figs. 10, 20; Appendix E). Table 4 records policy-enforced overall attack counts of 11, 11, 1, 0, 0, and 1 for the six models in table order. Their locations matter: Claude/Flash residuals are Travel; o4's residual is Banking. No blanket zero statement fits all those rows.

Fig. 10 conditions its denominator on successfully solved tasks; Fig. 20 uses all tasks. Workspace generally triggers less often because identity/readership annotations are clearer. Slack identity ambiguity, untrusted web sources, and strict Banking rules increase triggers. The experiment measures enforcement frequency, not whether real people correctly approve requests.

### X6 — Baseline-defense comparison

[A] With Claude 3.5 Sonnet, CaMeL is compared with prompt sandwiching, spotlighting, tool filter, and an undefended agent (Fig. 11; Tables 5–7). Table 7 counts are CaMeL 0, no-policy CaMeL 1, sandwiching 24, spotlighting 5, filter 8, undefended 44. The prose calls tool filter the next best defense despite spotlighting's lower tabulated count. CaMeL has markedly lower utility than spotlighting in this older-model experiment. Security and utility should be judged jointly, not merged into a single ranking.

### X7 — Data-driven action dispatcher

[A/B] Section 6.4 and Appendix H.3 examine generated code that extracts action names and parameters from emails, then chooses among available tool branches. The authors explicitly weaponize and simplify the main-text example; it is not identical to the original model output. Isolation alone permits data to act like instructions when the generated plan already contains a general dispatcher. This is a qualitative attack construction, not a reported success-rate trial.

### X8 — Overhead and mode comparison

[A] Token distributions and absolute counts appear in Fig. 13, Fig. 21, Tables 10–13. Tables 8–9 compare NORMAL/STRICT trigger rates: 33.87/53.23% benign overall and 26.54/45.34% under attack. No measured wall-clock latency, memory, or throughput table is provided. The description of small interpreter overhead is an author statement, not a quantitative timing result.

### X9 — Side channels and stronger threats

[A] Figs. 14–16 demonstrate request-count, exception-termination, and timing channels. Appendix I gives a generated meeting-summary plan that may leak whether the user's calendar contains a meeting with Bob. Fig. 17 discusses spy tools and rogue users. These are analytical examples, distinct from aggregate AgentDojo evaluation, and their real-world prevalence is not measured.

## 9. Results

[A] The strongest principal benign result is o3 High completing 77.3% ± 8.3 with CaMeL versus 84.5% ± 7.2 with native calling (Table 2). [C] Using displayed values, 84.5 − 77.3 = 7.2 percentage points. This is not a 7.2% relative decrease. For o4 Mini High the analogous gap is 79.4 − 76.3 = 3.1 points. For Gemini Pro it is 73.2 − 41.2 = 32.0 points. Thus utility preservation varies substantially with model and suite.

## 12. Diagram / architecture interpretation

Figures 1–2 define the core security boundary: an approved workflow can have unapproved arguments. Notes provide both recipient and document name; Drive supplies document contents; email delivery combines them. The attacker does not need to add a tool to cause harm. Fig. 5's architecture therefore routes untrusted material to a powerless parser, keeps the planner's context restricted, and assigns enforcement to the interpreter. The interpreter joins data dependencies with per-value rights at each tool boundary.

Figs. 7 and 19 reveal a second boundary: information can flow through a decision to act. In STRICT mode, the send operation depends on the classification result and its date/email inputs. In NORMAL, that influence is absent from the graph. Figs. 14–15 show why the missing edge matters: observers can infer a secret from call frequency or whether a later call happens.

Fig. 12 illustrates repeated action selection inside a fixed plan. A loop plus a list of permitted branches can become a small instruction interpreter whose choices originate in emails. [D] For web-agent security, this means validating the outer plan alone may not stop a malicious page from controlling behavior indirectly through parsed action labels. Policies must constrain the authority of those values, not merely the syntactic availability of tools.

Fig. 17 separates two extensions: a third-party tool receiving protected data and a user intentionally requesting forbidden disclosure. The enforcement goal is organizational policy, beyond the main trusted-user prompt-injection model. These diagrams establish mechanisms and design requirements; they do not provide empirical deployment results.

## 13. Equations and mathematical concepts

### ALG1 / Figure 3 — PI-SEC

[A] The game takes adversary A, Agent, and tools. It samples `(prompt, Ω_prompt)` from P, lets A choose an adversarial initial memory `mem*`, and obtains `Trace = Agent(prompt, tools, mem*)`. Each trace element is `(tool, args, mem_step)`: invoked operation, arguments, and state at execution. Verification succeeds exactly when every element belongs to Ω_prompt.

The central predicate can be represented as `Verify(Trace, Ω) = true iff every (tool, args, mem_step) in Trace belongs to Ω`. This restates the supplied pseudocode rather than introducing a new theorem. Ω_prompt is the set of allowed actions for the prompt. P is the prompt/allowed-action sampling source; the paper does not specify its probability distribution in detail. The adversary wins when an executed tuple lies outside Ω_prompt. The symbol `$` on the sampling arrow indicates randomized sampling; `∈` is membership, and `∉` non-membership.

This definition concerns allowed operations, not answer accuracy. A wrong displayed summary can escape the metric if it causes no prohibited flow. Footnote 4 explicitly states that Ω_prompt belongs to the security definition, not the actual CaMeL design. The implementation avoids exhaustively listing all acceptable actions for every possible request.

### ALG2 / Figure 4 — Policy gate

[A] Initialize Trace empty; add Q-LLM to tools; obtain a plan from the P-LLM; check each `(tool, args)` against policies and current memory. If the check returns `⊥`, representing rejection, halt and return the current trace. Otherwise run the tool, update memory, and add the operation to the trace. This expresses prevention at the tool boundary. It does not constitute a proof that every Python interpreter path implements the predicate correctly.

### Dependency tracking

[A] For `c = a + b`, c inherits dependence on a and b. A variable's complete dependency graph is obtained recursively. STRICT adds conditional/iterable influence and subsequent Q-LLM-input dependence. [D] This captures selected implicit flows but does not show a complete mathematical noninterference proof: the authors separately acknowledge residual exceptions and timing channels.

[A] Appendix A.1.1 uses `Ax + b = y` to argue that model parameters and data are mathematically intertwined. A and b are described as control-related, x as data, and y as output. ## 14. Interpretation and discussion

[A] The results support the authors' central design argument: model robustness and system enforcement are different properties. A parser can remain manipulable while a policy layer stops its output from initiating a forbidden operation. The architecture reduces reliance on the model as the final security decision-maker. The paper also supports combining CaMeL with model-oriented defenses rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.

[D, MEDIUM] The most defensible answer to the user's question is that web agents add pathways connecting untrusted content to privileged actions. In the paper's conventional tool loop, outside content returns into the same context that chooses later tools. A page or document can influence recipient selection, file selection, payment details, and branching. Multi-step composition adds opportunities for individual outputs to become later inputs. External services additionally make behavior observable, enabling leakage even when direct secret-bearing arguments are blocked.

However, this is a mechanism-based inference. The study compares native tool-calling agents with CaMeL agents. It does not hold a model constant and experimentally compare text-only interaction against web-enabled interaction. It does not report web-agent vulnerability ratios or establish that the model itself becomes easier to manipulate. The added danger includes expanded authority and consequences, which are distinct from intrinsic prompt-injection susceptibility.

## 15. Contributions and novelty

[A] **Conceptual:** secure an agent by designing its environment and authority boundaries, rather than requiring the model to learn perfect resistance. **Methodological:** distinguish control-flow hijacking from harmful manipulation of data arguments. **System:** combine isolated model roles, a restricted interpreter, provenance, reader capabilities, and flexible tool policies. **Implementation:** generate executable plans, preserve tagged state through repair, redact untrusted errors, and track selected implicit dependencies in STRICT mode.

[A] **Formalization:** define PI-SEC as an allowed-action trace game. This is a security definition, not a supplied formal verification of the complete implementation. **Empirical:** compare models, isolation-only and policy-enforced conditions, baseline defenses, utility failures, and overhead. **Analytical:** identify data-driven dispatchers and side channels that complicate simple isolation claims.

[A] The authors claim the first concrete Dual LLM instantiation and previously unconsidered capability use for agents, with knowledge-qualified wording. This report preserves those as author novelty claims and does not independently establish priority. No new dataset or benchmark is claimed; AgentDojo is reused.

## 16. Limitations

### Authors' stated limitations

[A] Text-only answer manipulation and phishing are outside the main protection goal. Users may need clarification or explicit approval. The planner cannot directly reason over tool content; data-dependent tasks, missing parser context, and undocumented APIs reduce utility. Restricted-language errors require repeated repair. There is no rollback or atomicity for side-effect sequences. Side channels can leak information, and STRICT does not cover every possible tool-induced exception or timing mechanism.

[A] Policies must be specified and maintained, correct annotations must be available, third-party integrations may require substantial adaptation, and ecosystem capability support can be difficult. Declassification and repetitive approval prompts can fatigue users. Composing permitted actions could create malicious overall behavior. The authors explicitly reject claims that prompt injection or AgentDojo is fully solved. Formal interpreter verification remains future work.

### Additional evidence-based analyst observations

[D] Several important numerical statements conflict with tables or captions. Run counts and the meaning of ± are not adequately specified in the supplied text. Benchmark identity/permission information varies across suites, affecting policy granularity. The older-model failure examples are lengthy and sometimes mislabeled. A Q-LLM on p. 122 infers French cuisine despite empty cuisine metadata; this suggests structured output does not guarantee extraction from supplied evidence, but it is one transcript rather than a measured hallucination rate.

[D] The user-origin provenance assigned to generated literals is an architectural convention; it does not prove that the P-LLM faithfully represents the user's intent. The abstract's strongest utility number is model-specific and should not stand for every evaluated model. The stronger-user and spy-tool scenarios are not experimentally validated here. None of these observations establishes a new working exploit; they identify limits of the evidence and assurance argument.

## 17. Threats to validity

The following labels are analyst classifications, not necessarily the authors' terminology.

**Internal validity [D, MEDIUM].** Native and CaMeL paths differ in prompting, programming, parsing, repair, and authority handling. Their utility differences cannot be attributed solely to capability checks. Changing model generations across experiments also complicates comparisons. Policies sometimes appear to be evaluated separately from utility, and confirmation handling is unclear.

**Construct validity [D, MEDIUM].** Benchmark attacker success can count displaying an injected hotel name as success even when no prohibited action occurs. Conversely, attacks outside the tool-action game can remain harmful to users. Utility checks may penalize a substantively correct answer lacking a particular word, as H.4.8 reports. Attack success, policy compliance, factual accuracy, and useful autonomy are separate constructs.

**External/ecological validity [D, MEDIUM].** Four benchmark suites do not cover the full open web, arbitrary browser interfaces, changing access rights, tool ecosystems, or human approval behavior. Section 8 examples are plausible author-described scenarios but not deployment measurements. The paper gives no standalone-versus-web experiment, so generalized relative vulnerability remains unquantified.

**Statistical conclusion validity [D, LOW for significance claims].** Tables include uncertainty and plots show bars, but their definitions, repetitions, tests, and significance thresholds are not supplied. Words such as significantly should be read as author wording rather than an independently confirmed statistical test. Contradictory counts and overhead conditions further limit exact inference.

**Reproducibility [D, MEDIUM].** Model identifiers, prompts, tool schemas, policy sketches, and code-release links improve transparency. Missing benchmark revision, API settings, seeds, hardware, uncertainty calculation, and the uninspected repository prevent a complete reproduction assessment. The supplied source hash is an identifier provided by the user, not independently recomputed.

### A. Future work explicitly proposed by the authors

[A] Use a language with more explicit errors and input/output, such as Haskell, to reduce Python/exception complexity. Formally verify the interpreter, policy enforcement, and conflict resolution. ## 22. Very simple explanation — Explain Like I'm 15

Imagine an assistant that can read your messages and send files for you. A stranger puts a message inside a document saying to send your private file to their address. The assistant may confuse that message with an instruction. Because it has useful tools, the mistake can become an actual email or payment rather than just a wrong sentence.

CaMeL separates the jobs. One AI writes a plan from your request. Another reads the outside material but cannot operate tools. A software supervisor remembers where each piece of information came from and who is allowed to receive it. Before sending anything or changing something, that supervisor checks the rules. Even if the reading AI gets fooled, a forbidden action can be stopped.

The paper also shows why simply separating the two AIs is not enough. The reader could return the wrong email address, or a plan could contain many possible actions and let the document choose one. CaMeL therefore checks how information is used, including some situations where a secret affects whether an action happens.

The tests show much better resistance to the benchmark's attacks, but useful performance varies, the system costs more tokens, and some information can still leak through behavior. People must write good rules, and the implementation has not yet been formally proved correct. For web agents, the important lesson is that reading an untrusted page becomes more dangerous when the assistant can turn what it reads into actions on your behalf. The paper explains that mechanism; it does not measure how many times more vulnerable an agent is than a standalone model.

claims.statement: Agentic interaction with untrusted tool outputs and web pages exposes LLM systems to prompt injections that can exfiltrate data or cause harmful actions.
Dual-model isolation protects planning but can leave tool arguments vulnerable to manipulation through the quarantined model's outputs.

CaMeL combines a privileged code-generating model, a tool-free quarantined parser, a provenance-tracking interpreter, per-value capabilities, and tool-time security policies without modifying the underlying LLM.
The main threat model assumes a trusted user prompt and uncompromised memory; text-only manipulation and phishing without protected-flow consequences are explicit non-goals.

Table 2 reports benign overall utility of 77.3% ± 8.3 for o3 High with CaMeL versus 84.5% ± 7.2 with native tool calling; the meaning of the uncertainty terms is not specified in the supplied methods.

In the Claude 3.5 Sonnet baseline comparison, Table 7 reports zero successful attacks for policy-enforced CaMeL, five for spotlighting, eight for tool filter, 24 for prompt sandwiching, and 44 for the undefended agent; these are benchmark counts, not standalone-LLM comparisons.

STRICT mode mitigates selected implicit-flow and Q-LLM exception channels by propagating dependencies, but CaMeL remains subject to possible side-channel leakage and does not establish universal confidentiality.
The supplied implementation is not formally verified; the authors identify proof of interpreter correctness and intended policy enforcement as future work.

For the research question, the paper supports a mechanism-based inference that web agents add dangerous pathways from untrusted content to privileged actions and observable external effects; it does not directly measure relative vulnerability against standalone LLMs.

Token overhead is reported inconsistently: the main text/Figure 13 state median input/output multipliers 2.82×/2.73×, while explicitly adversarial Table 13 gives 2.02×/2.64×; the supplied work does not resolve the discrepancy.
A fixed generated plan can still implement a dispatcher in which untrusted email data chooses actions, making isolation alone insufficient for such delegated workflows.
CaMeL does not fully solve prompt injection or AgentDojo; the authors retain policy-maintenance, human-approval, side-channel, and compositional limitations.

limitations: Pages 1–125 were available as supplied extracted text; direct source-image inspection covered pages 1–56 only.
All Figures 1–21 and Tables 1–14 were within the visual range, but tiny individual cells in Table 14 were not fully transcribed.
No tools, browsing, OCR, repository inspection, code execution, external verification, or hash recomputation were performed.
The source conflicts on Gemini Pro attack count, next-best baseline ranking, misunderstanding count, token overhead values/conditions, and some appendix labels.
The meaning of most reported plus/minus terms, run repetitions, seeds, benchmark revision, and several evaluation settings is not established by the supplied material.
Long repetitive transcripts, secondary table cells, API method lists, references, and decorative material are deliberately compressed with disclosure.
Research relevance is analyst inference; the paper does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web AI agents.
Formal verification is future work, and stated security guarantees remain conditional on policies, annotations, enforcement correctness, trust assumptions, and side-channel boundaries.

research.title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper explains mechanisms by which tool-using web agents connect untrusted pages, messages, and tool outputs to privileged actions, sensitive data, and externally observable behavior. These mechanisms support an architectural explanation of increased attack exposure and potential harm. The experiments compare native tool-calling agents against CaMeL agents, not agents against standalone LLMs; no relative standalone-versus-web vulnerability rate is established.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Untrusted tool outputs, web pages, emails, shared documents, spreadsheets, extracted tool arguments, data-driven dispatch branches, error feedback, and behavioral side channels. Main assumptions trust the user prompt and memory. Malicious tools and rogue users are discussed as stronger conceptual scenarios outside the explicit AgentDojo evaluation.
research.method: CaMeL separates a privileged code-generating planner from a tool-free quarantined parser, executes restricted Python through a custom interpreter, propagates provenance and permitted-reader capabilities, and checks policies before tool execution. NORMAL and STRICT dependency modes are evaluated alongside AgentDojo utility, attack counts, policy triggers, baseline defenses, failure examples, and token overhead.
research.limitations: No direct standalone comparison; text-only manipulation and phishing are non-goals; utility loss varies substantially by model/suite; policies and annotations require maintenance; user approval can cause fatigue; partial side effects lack rollback; side channels remain possible; interpreter formal verification is future work; several numbers and appendix labels conflict; uncertainty and repetition reporting is incomplete; source-code artifacts were not supplied or inspected.
